n6-licao-probes.titulo: The building manager who knocks on the door: probes
n6-licao-probes.enunciado:
Kubernetes knows whether the process is running, but not whether it is working. That’s what probes are for: checks the kubelet runs on each container:

  • readinessProbe: “can it take customers?” While it fails, the pod stays out of the Service’s endpoints (READY 0/1), but it isn’t restarted. This is what lets an update go out with no errors for customers.
  • livenessProbe: “is it alive?” If it fails several times in a row (failureThreshold), the container is restarted. It’s for a hung program, one that keeps running without answering.
  • startupProbe: “has it finished starting up?” Until it passes, the other two wait. For apps that are slow to start, without having to loosen the liveness probe.
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:              # or tcpSocket: { port: 8080 }, or exec: { command: [...] }
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 0
  periodSeconds: 10     # how often
  failureThreshold: 3   # how many failures in a row before acting

Where to look: kubectl describe pod NAME shows the probes (Liveness:, Readiness:) and, in the Events, every failure (Unhealthy) and every liveness restart (Killing).

The classic gotcha: a tight liveness probe on a program that is slow to start kills the container before it gets ready, forever (CrashLoopBackOff). Use a startupProbe.
n6-licao-probes.vidaReal: Every so often the building manager stops by and asks: “anyone alive in there?” (liveness), “can you take customers?” (readiness) and, on the first day, “done with the move?” (startup).
n6-licao-probes.limite: The building manager only knows what the door answers: if the answer lies (always “all good”), they don’t notice the problem.

n6-licao-recursos.titulo: The contracted power and the circuit breaker: requests and limits
n6-licao-recursos.enunciado:
resources:
  requests:        # what the scheduler reserves on the node
    cpu: 250m      # 250 millicores = a quarter of a CPU
    memory: 128Mi
  limits:          # the maximum
    cpu: 500m      # go over it: the container gets slower (throttling)
    memory: 256Mi  # go over it: the container is killed (OOMKilled)
  • requests: the scheduler only places the pod on a node where the sum of requests fits. A request that’s too big = a Pending pod (Insufficient cpu).
  • memory limits: go over, and the kernel kills the container, the reason becomes OOMKilled (exit code 137) and it restarts (and goes into CrashLoopBackOff if it keeps happening).
  • CPU limits: the container doesn’t die, it just gets capped: kubectl top shows it stuck at the limit.

QoS classes

When a node runs out of memory, whoever asked for the least guarantee goes first: BestEffort (nothing declared), then Burstable (something declared) and last Guaranteed (requests = limits, for CPU and memory, in every container). See it in kubectl describe pod NAME, on the QoS Class line.

How much each one uses

kubectl top pods and kubectl top nodes show current usage. The one measuring it is the metrics-server, which kind doesn’t ship installed (without it: Metrics API not available); the clusters in this level already come with it.
n6-licao-recursos.vidaReal: The request is the contracted power: the building only takes the resident if the grid can handle it. The limit is the circuit breaker: go over on memory and it trips (the container dies); on CPU, the lights just dim (it gets slow).
n6-licao-recursos.limite: On the power grid, everyone can draw more than they contracted at the same time and the building goes dark; in Kubernetes, the request is really reserved on the node.

n6-licao-escala.titulo: Black Friday temps and the condo quota
n6-licao-escala.enunciado:
HorizontalPodAutoscaler

kubectl autoscale deployment loja --cpu=50% --min=2 --max=8

The HPA looks at the pods’ CPU usage as a percentage of the request and computes replicas = ⌈current replicas × usage / target⌉. That’s why the pods need requests: without them, the target shows <unknown> and nothing happens. Watch it with kubectl get hpa -w.

Careful: the HPA changes the Deployment’s spec.replicas. If your YAML also sets replicas, every apply fights with it.

ResourceQuota and LimitRange

  • ResourceQuota: a namespace’s ceiling (pods, requests and limits added up). A pod that goes over is refused (exceeded quota), and, with a CPU or memory quota, every container must declare requests and limits (must specify).
  • LimitRange: default values for whoever declared nothing, plus minimums and maximums per container.

When a Deployment can’t create pods, the error doesn’t show up on apply: it’s in the ReplicaSet’s Events (kubectl describe rs, FailedCreate). See the usage with kubectl describe quota.
n6-licao-escala.vidaReal: The HPA is the temp-staff manager, who hires temps when the line grows and lets them go when things calm down. The ResourceQuota is each company’s power quota in the condo; the LimitRange, the rules for whoever shows up without saying how much they’ll use.
n6-licao-escala.limite: The manager is slow: checks the line every 15 seconds and waits 5 minutes before letting anyone go (so as not to fire and rehire every minute).

n6-pronto-para-atender.titulo: Update with zero errors, for real
n6-pronto-para-atender.enunciado: Version 2.1 of loja (kubelearn/loja:2.1-aquece) warms up its cache for 20 seconds before serving. Update loja to it without a single customer getting an error: a customer will request http://loja every second during the switch. When it’s ready, loja answers 200 on /healthz (port 8080).
n6-pronto-para-atender.dica: Change the image and add a readinessProbe httpGet on /healthz, port 8080. Without it, the new pod counts as ready before it opens the port.
n6-pronto-para-atender.vidaReal: The new clerk arrives, but is still booting up the computer. Without the question “can you serve yet?”, the front gate already sends customers their way.
n6-pronto-para-atender.limite: Readiness only protects traffic coming through the Service: anyone talking straight to the pod’s IP skips the building manager.
n6-pronto-para-atender.comoSaber: During the switch, kubectl get pods -w: the new pods stay 0/1 for about 20 seconds.

testes.descricao: the switch to 2.1 with no errors for customers

n6-loja-travada.enunciado: After about 40 seconds up, loja freezes: the process keeps running, the pod stays Running, but requests go unanswered (check the logs). Make Kubernetes notice and restart the frozen container.
n6-loja-travada.vidaReal: The clerk is in the chair, eyes open, but doesn’t answer anyone. From the outside, everything looks normal.
n6-loja-travada.limite: Restarting fixes the symptom, not the cause: the deadlock comes back. Liveness buys time until someone fixes the program.
n6-loja-travada.comoSaber: kubectl get pods -w: the RESTARTS column goes up; kubectl describe pod NAME shows Container loja failed liveness probe, will be restarted.

testes.descricao: the kubelet restarts the frozen loja

msgs.1: the kubelet killed a container because of the liveness probe

n6-subida-lenta.titulo: The store that takes a while to wake up
n6-subida-lenta.enunciado: Version 3.0 of loja migrates the database when it starts (about 45 seconds). Its livenessProbe is tight, and the pods never leave CrashLoopBackOff. Without loosening the liveness probe, get loja up.
n6-subida-lenta.dica: A startupProbe (httpGet /healthz, port 8080) with failureThreshold × periodSeconds greater than 45 seconds: until it passes, the liveness probe waits.
n6-subida-lenta.vidaReal: The building manager knocks 3 times in 15 seconds and, with no answer, breaks the door down. But the move takes 45 seconds: they break in every time, and the move never finishes.
n6-subida-lenta.limite: You could loosen the liveness probe (initialDelaySeconds), but then a real freeze also takes longer to notice.

n6-pergunta-errada.enunciado: The loja pods are Running, but 0/1, and the loja Service has no endpoints. Find the reason in the Events (kubectl describe pod NAME) and fix it. loja reports its health on /healthz.
n6-pergunta-errada.dica: The readinessProbe asks on a path loja doesn’t know (404).
n6-pergunta-errada.vidaReal: To find out whether the store has opened, the building manager asks “is the meeting room free?”: the answer is always “no idea”, and the store never opens.
n6-pergunta-errada.limite: A wrong readiness probe doesn’t take anything down: it just quietly keeps the pod out of the Service, which sometimes takes a while for anyone to notice.

n6-potencia-demais.enunciado: One of the 3 loja pods is Pending. Check the reason (kubectl describe pod NAME, under Events) and how much loja really uses (kubectl top pods). Adjust the request so all 3 fit.
n6-potencia-demais.dica: resources.requests.cpu: 1500m is too much. loja uses just a few millicores; 250m is plenty.
n6-potencia-demais.vidaReal: Each store asked for 1.5 kW of contracted power, but each building only has 2 kW: the third store doesn’t fit anywhere.
n6-potencia-demais.limite: The request isn’t what the program uses: it’s what gets reserved. The store uses far less, and the reservation still takes up the space.

n6-disjuntor.enunciado: The relatorio (report) keeps restarting. Find the reason (kubectl describe pod NAME: the Last State and the Reason) and fix it. The report loads a spreadsheet of about 300Mi.
n6-disjuntor.dica: OOMKilled: the container went over limits.memory. Raise the limit (512Mi leaves some room).
n6-disjuntor.vidaReal: The report turns on the AC, the oven and the shower at the same time on a 10 A circuit breaker: it trips every time.
n6-disjuntor.limite: A bigger circuit breaker fixes it if the report really needs that much; if it leaks memory, it only delays the crash.
n6-disjuntor.comoSaber: kubectl get pods: 1/1 Running and the restarts stop.

n6-garantido.enunciado: Give the caixa-forte (vault) pod the Guaranteed QoS: the last one out when the node runs out of memory.
n6-garantido.dica: requests and limits equal, for both cpu and memory.
n6-garantido.vidaReal: During a blackout, the generators serve those who contracted guaranteed power first.
n6-garantido.limite: Guaranteed isn’t immortal: a Guaranteed pod still dies if it goes over its own memory limit.
n6-garantido.comoSaber: kubectl describe pod caixa-forte shows QoS Class: Guaranteed.

n6-quem-gasta.enunciado: Which pod in the default namespace is using the most memory?
n6-quem-gasta.vidaReal: The electricity bill came in high: the building manager checks each apartment’s meter.
n6-quem-gasta.limite: The meter shows right now, not the history: for yesterday’s peak, you need a monitoring tool (Prometheus).

n6-autoscale.enunciado: From the terminal, create an HPA for deployment/loja: a target of 50% CPU, minimum 2 and maximum 6 replicas.
n6-autoscale.vidaReal: Hiring a manager with the rule: “keep the clerks busy half the time, with at least 2 and at most 6”.
n6-autoscale.limite: The manager only hires if there’s room: with no space on the nodes, the temps wait at the door (Pending).
n6-autoscale.comoSaber: kubectl get hpa shows cpu: N%/50%, MINPODS 2 and MAXPODS 6.

n6-black-friday.enunciado: Black Friday has started: the carga (load) pod is sending requests nonstop to loja, and the HPA exists, but loja is still at 2 replicas. kubectl get hpa shows <unknown>. Find the reason (kubectl describe hpa loja) and make the HPA work.
n6-black-friday.dica: The HPA computes CPU as a percentage of the request: loja needs resources.requests.cpu (100m, for example). Don’t write replicas in the Deployment: the HPA is in charge of them now.
n6-black-friday.vidaReal: The manager got the order “keep the clerks at 50% of capacity”, but nobody said what each one’s capacity is: they can’t do the math and don’t hire anyone.
n6-black-friday.limite: The HPA reacts in minutes, not seconds: for a sudden spike, it’s good to start with some headroom (minReplicas).
n6-black-friday.comoSaber: kubectl get hpa -w: the target stops being <unknown> and the replicas go up.

msgs.2: the HPA can measure the CPU

n6-cota.enunciado: In the vendas namespace, the loja Deployment can’t create any pods. Find the reason (kubectl describe rs -n vendas, under Events, and kubectl describe quota -n vendas) and fix the Deployment so it fits within the quota.
n6-cota.dica: The quota has requests.cpu and limits.memory: every container must declare both. Each loja pod can ask for 250m of CPU and a 256Mi memory limit.
n6-cota.vidaReal: The condo gave the Vendas (Sales) company a power quota and requires every appliance to come with an energy label. An appliance without a label doesn’t get in.
n6-cota.limite: The quota adds up what’s declared, not what’s used: an exaggerated request takes up quota even with the store idle.

testes.descricao: the vendas loja opens within the quota

n6-regras-padrao.titulo: The rules for whoever shows up without a label
n6-regras-padrao.enunciado: The compras namespace has a quota that requires requests and limits, and the team doesn’t want to touch every Deployment. Create a LimitRange named padrao that gives every container with nothing declared: a request of 100m CPU and 64Mi memory, and a limit of 250m and 128Mi. The compras loja must start without changing the Deployment.
n6-regras-padrao.dica: kind LimitRange, spec.limits with type Container, defaultRequest and default.
n6-regras-padrao.vidaReal: Instead of turning away every appliance without a label, the management office sticks a default label on at the entrance.
n6-regras-padrao.limite: The default applies to everyone: an appliance that uses much more than the default will trip the circuit breaker (the default limit).
n6-regras-padrao.comoSaber: kubectl get pods -n compras: 2 pods Running (the ReplicaSet retries on its own, within a few seconds).

testes.descricao: the compras loja starts with the default rules

n6-teto.enunciado: The loja in compras doesn’t create any pods (check the ReplicaSet’s Events in the compras namespace). Fix the Deployment.
n6-teto.dica: The namespace’s LimitRange has a memory max of 512Mi: loja’s limits.memory has to fit.
n6-teto.vidaReal: The condo rule says: no appliance with a circuit breaker above 512. Yours came with 1000.
n6-teto.limite: The ceiling is per container; to cap the namespace’s total, use the quota (ResourceQuota).
